glossary.definition: A geographic Azure location containing one or more datacenters connected by a high-capacity network.
A physically separate set of datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking.
A logical container used to organize and manage related Azure resources.
An Azure billing and management boundary that contains resource groups and resources.
Virtual network: a logically isolated Azure network where resources can communicate through private IP addressing.
A network-access point through which a client reaches a service.
Domain Name System: the system that resolves human-readable names to network records.
Single sign-on: one authenticated session can provide access to multiple authorized applications.
Multifactor authentication: authentication that uses factors from more than one category, such as something you know plus something you have or are.
Role-based access control: authorization based on a principal, a role, and a scope.
A security approach based on explicit verification, least privilege, and assuming that compromise can happen.
Application programming interface: a defined way for software to request functions or data from another software system.
Internet Protocol address: a network address used to identify where traffic should be sent.

modules.title: Build the Azure architecture mental model

reveal.text: An Azure datacenter is a physical facility that contains computing, networking, and storage infrastructure. An Azure region is a geographic area that contains one or more datacenters connected by a high-capacity network.
A resource's region can affect latency, data residency, service availability, and price. Many Azure resources are created in a specific region.
Datacenter is the physical facility. Region is the larger Azure location you normally select when deploying a regional resource.

reveal.text: An Availability Zone is a physically separate set of datacenters within an Azure region. Each zone has independent power, cooling, and networking to reduce the chance that one datacenter-level failure affects every zone.
Use zone-aware services or place redundant workload components across zones when the application needs protection from a datacenter-level failure within one region.
Availability Zones provide fault isolation inside one region. A multi-region design protects against a broader regional failure.

nodes.title: Region pairs, nonpaired regions, and sovereign regions

reveal.text: Microsoft associates some Azure regions with another region to form a region pair. A small number of services use region pairs for geo-replication, geo-redundancy, or parts of disaster recovery, but many newer regions are not paired.
Sovereign Azure environments are separated cloud environments designed for specific government, national, or regulatory requirements. Examples include Azure Government and Azure China.

prompts.label: DO NOT ASSUME EVERY REGION IS PAIRED

reveal.text: A resilient design does not require a paired region. Azure has paired and nonpaired regions, and many services support multi-region resilience independently of region pairing.

reveal.text: An Azure resource is an instance of a service you create, such as a virtual machine, storage account, or virtual network. A resource group is a logical container used to organize and manage related Azure resources.
You can apply management actions, access control, policy, tags, or lifecycle operations at a resource-group scope so related resources can be managed together.
If the requirement is to organize several Azure resources and manage them as a logical unit, think resource group.

reveal.text: An Azure subscription is a management and billing boundary that contains Azure resource groups and resources. Access, quotas, and cost tracking can be organized at the subscription level.
Organizations often separate subscriptions to create different billing, access, quota, or environment boundaries, such as separating production from experimentation.
A resource group organizes resources inside a subscription. A subscription is the larger billing and management boundary that contains resource groups.

nodes.title: Management groups and the Azure hierarchy

reveal.text: A management group is a management scope above subscriptions. It lets an organization apply governance and access rules across multiple subscriptions.
When a governance rule must apply across many subscriptions, use a higher management-group scope. Settings assigned at a parent scope can affect resources beneath that scope.

reveal.text: Azure virtual machines provide a full guest operating system. Containers package an application and its dependencies into a lightweight isolated unit. Functions run event-driven code without you managing servers.

cells.fit: Legacy/custom server software or OS-level control
Portable packaged services with faster startup than full VMs
Event-driven or short units of work

reveal.text: Need the OS: VM. Need a portable packaged app: container. Need event-driven code with minimal infrastructure management: function.

nodes.title: Azure VM options: VMs, scale sets, availability sets, and Virtual Desktop

prompts.label: WHY ARE THERE SEVERAL VM OPTIONS?

reveal.text: Azure provides different VM-based options for a single server, a scalable group of servers, failure-aware placement, or hosted desktops. The correct choice depends on whether the goal is compute capacity, scale, availability, or user desktops.

cells.purpose: Create and manage a scalable group of similar VMs
Spread VMs across fault and update domains to reduce correlated failures
Deliver virtual Windows desktops and applications to users

prompts.label: SCALE IS NOT THE SAME AS DESKTOP VIRTUALIZATION

reveal.text: VM Scale Sets are about groups of VM instances and scaling. Azure Virtual Desktop is about delivering desktop and application sessions to users.

nodes.title: Resources a virtual machine depends on

prompts.label: WHAT DOES A VM NEED AROUND IT?

reveal.text: An Azure VM is more than CPU and memory. Supporting resources include disks and a network interface connected to a virtual network and subnet. A public IP address is optional.

items: VM size: determines compute capacity such as processor cores and memory.
Managed disks: store the operating system and optional data.
Network interface: connects the VM to a virtual network and subnet.
Public IP address: optional when direct public connectivity is required.

reveal.text: A VM question may include the VM itself plus disks, networking, and an optional public IP. Do not assume every VM needs a public IP.

nodes.title: Application hosting: Web Apps, containers, or VMs

reveal.text: Application hosting determines how much of the runtime and operating environment your team manages. Azure Web Apps is a managed web-hosting platform, containers package the application runtime, and VMs expose the full guest operating system.

cells.clue: You want managed hosting for web apps or APIs without managing the OS.
You want a portable application image with its dependencies.
You need guest-OS control or software that expects a traditional server.

reveal.text: More control usually means more management. A VM gives the most OS control; Web Apps removes the most OS management of these three choices.

prompts.label: WHAT IS AN AZURE VIRTUAL NETWORK?

reveal.text: An Azure virtual network (VNet) is a logically isolated network in Azure. A subnet divides a VNet address space into smaller ranges so resources can be grouped and network controls can be applied more deliberately.
Use subnets to separate groups such as web, application, and data tiers or to place resources where different routing or network-security rules should apply.
VNet is the private network boundary. Subnet is a smaller address range inside that VNet.

reveal.text: Virtual network peering connects Azure VNets so resources can communicate privately across the Microsoft backbone while the VNets remain separate management objects.
Use peering when separate VNets need private connectivity, such as a hub network providing shared services to application networks.
Peering directly connects Azure VNets. VPN Gateway is commonly used to create encrypted tunnels across the public internet, including connections to on-premises networks.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals — skills measured as of July 20, 2026

reveal.text: Azure DNS is a managed Domain Name System (DNS) hosting service. DNS translates names such as app.example.com into the records clients need to locate a service.
Use Azure DNS when you want Azure to host DNS zones and records. You can manage them with the same Azure credentials, APIs, and tools used for other resources.

prompts.label: DNS DOES NOT CREATE NETWORK CONNECTIVITY

reveal.text: DNS answers name-resolution questions. It does not replace VNet routing, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, or other network paths.

reveal.text: Azure VPN Gateway carries encrypted traffic between networks over the public internet. Azure ExpressRoute provides private connectivity to Microsoft cloud services through a connectivity provider rather than sending that traffic over the public internet.

cells.path: Encrypted tunnel over the public internet
cells.clue: Secure hybrid connection without a dedicated private circuit

cells.path: Private connection through a connectivity provider

reveal.text: If the requirement explicitly says traffic should avoid the public internet for the hybrid connection, ExpressRoute is the stronger fit.

reveal.text: An endpoint is a network-access point for a service. A public endpoint is reached through a public address. An Azure Private Endpoint uses a private IP address from your VNet to connect to a supported service through Azure Private Link.
Use a private endpoint when a supported Azure service should be reachable from a VNet by private IP. This avoids using that service's public endpoint for the connection.
A subnet is an address range inside a VNet. A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP used to reach a supported service privately.

prompts.label: WHAT PROBLEM DOES AZURE STORAGE SOLVE?

reveal.text: Azure Storage provides managed services for several data shapes. The important AZ-900 skill is to recognize whether the workload needs object storage, shared files, messages, or simple NoSQL key-value-style data.

cells.fit: Shared SMB or NFS file access

reveal.text: Object, file, message, or NoSQL table is usually the fastest way to eliminate the wrong storage choices.

glossary.definition: Server Message Block: a common network file-sharing protocol used by Windows and other systems.
Network File System: a common network file-sharing protocol widely used by Linux and Unix-like systems.
A broad category of non-relational data models that do not require a traditional relational table schema.

nodes.title: Blob access tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive

reveal.text: A Blob Storage access tier changes the cost trade-off based on how often data is accessed. Hot, Cool, and Cold are online tiers; Archive is an offline tier intended for rarely accessed data that can tolerate rehydration delay.

cells.access: Rare access but still needs fast retrieval

reveal.text: If the data is almost never read and retrieval can wait, Archive fits. If it must remain immediately readable, choose an online tier based on access frequency.

reveal.text: Azure Storage redundancy keeps multiple copies of data. This reduces the chance that a hardware, datacenter, zone, or regional failure causes data loss or unavailability. The options differ by how widely the copies are distributed.

cells.copies: Within one physical location in the primary region
Across availability zones in the primary region
Primary region plus asynchronous copy to a secondary region
cells.goal: Regional durability; RA adds secondary read access

cells.copies: Across zones in primary region plus a secondary region
cells.goal: Zone resilience plus regional durability; RA adds secondary read access

prompts.label: DO NOT EQUATE GEO-REDUNDANCY WITH ACTIVE READS

reveal.text: GRS and GZRS replicate to a secondary region, but the secondary is not normally readable until failover. RA-GRS and RA-GZRS add read access to the secondary.

reveal.text: A storage account is the Azure resource that provides a namespace and configuration boundary for Azure Storage data services. Its account type, performance options, redundancy, and network settings determine what storage capabilities are available.
Before creating blobs, files, queues, or tables, you create or use a compatible storage account. General-purpose v2 accounts support the broadest set of common Azure Storage scenarios.
Do not confuse a storage account with the data inside it. The account is the management/configuration resource; containers, file shares, queues, and tables hold the data.

nodes.title: Move files: AzCopy, Storage Explorer, and Azure File Sync

reveal.text: AzCopy is a command-line data-transfer utility. Azure Storage Explorer is a graphical tool for working with Azure Storage. Azure File Sync synchronizes Azure file shares with Windows Server file servers.

cells.job: Script or automate high-performance copies to, from, or between Azure Storage locations
Browse and manage storage data with a desktop graphical interface
Keep Windows Server file shares synchronized with an Azure file share and optionally cache files locally

reveal.text: One-time or scripted copy: AzCopy. Human-friendly GUI: Storage Explorer. Ongoing server-to-Azure Files synchronization: Azure File Sync.

nodes.title: Azure Migrate and Azure Data Box

reveal.text: Azure Migrate is a service hub for discovering, assessing, and migrating workloads to Azure. Azure Data Box uses Microsoft-provided physical devices to move large amounts of data when network transfer is slow, expensive, or impractical.

columns.title: Azure Data Box
items: Useful when available network capacity is the limiting factor

reveal.text: If the scenario says there are terabytes or petabytes to move and the network is the bottleneck, Data Box is the clue. If the need is to assess and migrate servers or workloads, think Azure Migrate.

nodes.title: Microsoft Entra ID and Entra Domain Services

reveal.text: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity and access service. It stores identities and supports authentication and access to cloud applications and resources.

cells.purpose: Cloud identity, authentication, application access, and identity-based controls
Managed traditional domain services for workloads that need domain join and Active Directory-compatible protocols

reveal.text: Entra Domain Services is not a replacement name for Entra ID. It is a managed domain service for workloads that need traditional domain join and Active Directory-compatible behavior.

reveal.text: Single sign-on (SSO) lets one sign-in session provide access to multiple authorized applications. Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires factors from more than one authentication category. Passwordless authentication proves identity without relying on a reusable password.

cells.goal: Reduce repeated sign-ins across trusted applications
Require another factor so a stolen password alone is not enough
Avoid reusable passwords by using stronger methods such as passkeys, biometrics, or device-backed credentials

reveal.text: SSO is about convenience across apps. MFA is about multiple factors. Passwordless is about removing the password from the authentication flow.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals — skills measured as of July 20, 2026
Describe Azure identity, access, and security — Microsoft Learn

reveal.text: An external identity represents a user from outside your organization who needs controlled access to your applications or resources. Microsoft Entra supports collaboration with external users instead of creating an ordinary internal employee identity for every partner.
Use external identity and guest collaboration features when partners, vendors, or other organizations need access while keeping their own identity source.
Being invited as an external user does not automatically grant broad Azure permissions. Access still depends on application assignment, group membership, RBAC, and other controls.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals — skills measured as of July 20, 2026
Describe Azure identity, access, and security — Microsoft Learn

reveal.text: Microsoft Entra Conditional Access is a policy engine that evaluates identity and context signals and then enforces access requirements. A simple policy has an if-then shape: if specified conditions are true, require or block an access action.

items: Collect signals such as user, device, location, application, or risk
Allow, block, or require a control such as MFA

reveal.text: MFA is an authentication method. Conditional Access is the policy engine that can decide when MFA or another access control is required.

reveal.text: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) is Azure's authorization system for deciding who can perform which actions on which Azure resources.

prompts.label: A ROLE ASSIGNMENT HAS THREE PARTS

items: Role definition: what actions are allowed

prompts.label: SCOPE CAN BE NARROW OR BROAD

reveal.text: Azure RBAC can be assigned at management-group, subscription, resource-group, or resource scope. Choose the smallest scope that meets the access requirement.

reveal.text: Zero Trust is a security approach that does not automatically trust a request because it comes from a familiar network or location. Access decisions continuously consider identity, device, context, and the minimum permissions required.

items: Verify explicitly: use available signals to make access decisions.
Use least privilege: grant only the access needed for the task.
Assume breach: design so one compromised identity or component does not automatically expose everything.

reveal.text: A request to verify every access attempt, limit permissions, and assume compromise is describing Zero Trust.

reveal.text: Defense in depth uses multiple independent security layers so that one failed control does not expose the entire system. Protection can exist around identities, networks, compute, applications, and data.
No single security control stops every threat. Layering controls increases the chance that another control detects, blocks, or limits an attack when one layer fails.

prompts.label: NOT THE SAME AS ZERO TRUST

reveal.text: Zero Trust is an access and security strategy centered on explicit verification, least privilege, and assumed breach. Defense in depth is the broader idea of using multiple protective layers.

reveal.text: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud security service that helps assess security posture and protect workloads. It provides security recommendations and can surface threats across Azure and connected environments.
Use Defender for Cloud when teams need a central view of cloud security posture, recommendations to reduce risk, and workload-protection capabilities.
Defender for Cloud evaluates and improves security posture and workload protection. Azure RBAC grants or denies management actions based on role assignments.
